title: 1st Truth A Summary Of The Proofs Of Createdness And Contingency

questions.question: What are the two main ideas named in this passage as the First Truth?
questions.answer: They are createdness and contingency.

questions.question: Which groups of Muslim thinkers are said to have supported these two ideas with many proofs?
questions.answer: Scholars of Islamic belief and theology, along with Muslim sages.

questions.question: What observation about the world leads them to say the world is not eternal?
questions.answer: They see that things in the world keep changing and shifting.

questions.question: According to the passage, what follows if the world is created?
questions.answer: It must have a Maker.

questions.question: What does the passage say about a thing whose own essence does not require either its existence or its nonexistence?
questions.answer: Its existence is only possible, not necessary, so it is not eternal.

questions.question: Why does the passage connect contingency with the need for a Creator?
questions.answer: If things do not exist by necessity in themselves, then their existence must come from One who gives it to them.

questions.question: What is the main conclusion of the whole passage?
questions.answer: The changing and dependent world points to the existence of a Maker who is not created or dependent.

questions.question: What is being introduced by the heading “First Truth”?
questions.answer: A proof based on createdness and contingency.

questions.question: How does the passage describe the amount of evidence for this proof?
questions.answer: It says the evidence is countless.

questions.question: What feature of the world is directly noticed first in the argument?
questions.answer: The world shows ongoing change.

questions.question: Why does ongoing change matter in this argument?
questions.answer: Because it shows the world does not stay the same forever and so is not eternal in itself.

questions.question: What conclusion is drawn after saying the world is created?
questions.answer: That there is a Creator who made it.

questions.question: What does contingency mean here in simple words?
questions.answer: It means a thing could exist or not exist; its existence is not required by itself.

questions.question: If existence and nonexistence are equally possible for something, what does that say about it?
questions.answer: It is not necessary by itself.

questions.question: According to the passage, can a contingent thing be eternal by its own nature?
questions.answer: No, because it does not have existence from itself.

questions.question: How do createdness and contingency work together in the passage?
questions.answer: Createdness points to a beginning, and contingency shows dependence, so together they point to a Creator.

questions.question: What belief does this First Truth support?
questions.answer: It supports belief that the world has a Maker.

questions.question: What claim do Muslim theologians and sages make about the world in this passage?
questions.answer: They say the world is created and not uncreated.

questions.question: What evidence from everyday reality do they start with?
questions.answer: They start with the fact that things change.

questions.question: What does the passage say cannot be true about a changing world?
questions.answer: That it is uncreated and eternal in itself.

questions.question: What must exist if the world was brought into existence?
questions.answer: A Maker must exist.

questions.question: What does the passage teach about the inner nature of contingent things?
questions.answer: Their own nature does not make their existence necessary.

questions.question: If a thing could just as well not exist, what category does it belong to in this argument?
questions.answer: It belongs to the category of contingent things.

questions.question: Is the argument based on random guessing or on observed facts plus reasoning?
questions.answer: It is based on observed facts plus reasoning.

questions.question: What cause-and-effect chain appears in the passage from change to belief in a Maker?
questions.answer: Change shows the world is not eternal; if it is created, it needs a Creator.

questions.question: Give a short summary of the passage in one sentence.
questions.answer: Because the world changes and does not exist by itself, it must have been created by a Maker.

questions.question: What two terms should a student understand well to follow this passage?
questions.answer: Createdness and contingency.

questions.question: In simple language, what does contingency mean here?
questions.answer: It means something does not have to exist by itself and depends on another for existence.

questions.question: Who is said to have explained these ideas with many proofs?
questions.answer: Muslim scholars of theology and wise scholars of Islam.

questions.question: What sign in the world helps them argue that the world had a beginning?
questions.answer: The sign is constant change and transformation.

questions.question: Why does having a beginning point beyond the world itself?
questions.answer: Because what begins to exist needs one who brings it into existence.

questions.question: What does the passage say about something whose essence gives no reason for either existing or not existing?
questions.answer: It is only possible, not necessary or eternal.

questions.question: What bigger truth are these ideas meant to help prove?
questions.answer: That there is a Creator.

questions.question: How should a thoughtful reader respond to this passage?
questions.answer: By seeing that the changing world is dependent and reflects the need for a Maker.

questions.question: What is the first major proof in this passage built on?
questions.answer: It is built on createdness and contingency.

questions.question: What does the passage say scholars noticed about everything in the world?
questions.answer: They noticed change and alteration.

questions.question: From that observation, what did they conclude about the world itself?
questions.answer: They concluded that it is temporary and created.

questions.question: What false idea about the world is rejected by that conclusion?
questions.answer: The idea that the world is uncreated.

questions.question: What necessary conclusion comes after saying the world is created?
questions.answer: That it has a Creator.

questions.question: What does the passage mean when it says existence and nonexistence can be equal possibilities for a thing?
questions.answer: It means the thing does not exist by necessity in itself.

questions.question: Why is that important in the argument?
questions.answer: Because it shows the thing depends on another cause for existing.

questions.question: What can we infer about eternal existence from this passage?
questions.answer: Eternal necessary existence does not belong to changing, dependent things.

questions.question: What is one central lesson from the whole passage?
questions.answer: The world’s changing and dependent nature points to a Maker beyond it.

questions.question: What title is given to the section in the marked passage?
questions.answer: It is called the First Truth.

questions.question: What two truths are included in this section?
questions.answer: The truths of createdness and contingency.

questions.question: Whose work is mentioned as establishing these truths?
questions.answer: The work of Islamic theologians and Muslim sages.

questions.question: What fact about the world is treated as clear evidence in the passage?
questions.answer: That the world is full of change.

questions.question: What conclusion is reached from the fact that the world changes?
questions.answer: The world is not eternal in itself but created.

questions.question: Once the world is called created, what must also be accepted?
questions.answer: That there is a Maker who created it.

questions.question: What is the passage teaching about things that do not contain the reason for their own existence?
questions.answer: They are dependent and not necessary by themselves.

questions.question: Why are such things described as not eternal?
questions.answer: Because what is not necessary in itself cannot be everlasting by its own nature.

questions.question: Which idea in the passage is closer to “dependent existence”: createdness or contingency?
questions.answer: Contingency.

questions.question: How do the two parts of the argument strengthen each other?
questions.answer: One shows the world began, and the other shows it depends on another, so both support belief in a Creator.
